intro: The first movement of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, Op. 14, “Rêveries — Passions”, introduces the melody of the beloved, which returns in all five movements. Flute and violins first play it after a slow introduction broken by silences and sudden outbursts.

sections.label: Intro · Muted strings, slow C-minor opening
sections.mNote: A slow C-minor opening, broken by rests and fermatas

sections.label: A · Idée fixe, flute and first violins
sections.mNote: Flute and first violins play the idée fixe.

sections.label: A′ · Fragments of the beloved’s melody

cues.title: Opening bars, wind and muted violins
cues.text: Flute and clarinet begin quietly, repeating their notes as other wind instruments join them. Muted violins take up a melody with pauses, its phrases separated by fermatas. The strings play and fall silent several times.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Symphonie fantastique, movement I, bars 1–16; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 1–3: http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Romance from Florian’s Estelle
cues.text: Before leaving for Paris, Berlioz burned his early compositions, but he kept one melody in his memory. He had written it to words from Florian’s Estelle while grieving over his own adolescent love. Years later it became the violins’ melody in this introduction.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 4, describes the romance, its destruction and its reuse without alteration in the Largo: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: The “vague des passions”
cues.text: Berlioz’s programme gave the artist a “soul-sickness”, with melancholy and joys without cause, before he had ever seen her. It took the name for this, le vague des passions, from “a famous writer” whom it left unnamed. The writer was Chateaubriand.
cues.evidence: Berlioz’s 1845 programme, part I: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm . Michel Austin identifies the “famous writer” as Chateaubriand and relates the phrase to the opening of the symphony: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Beethoven in Paris, 1828
cues.text: In 1828 Habeneck’s new Conservatoire concerts brought Beethoven to Paris. Berlioz wrote that Beethoven “opened a new world in music”. After the C minor Symphony, Berlioz’s teacher Lesueur hurried out red-faced and said he was so shaken that he thought he could not find his head to put his hat on.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 20 (“Il m’ouvrait un monde nouveau en musique”; Lesueur after the symphony in C minor): https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/M%C3%A9moires_de_Hector_Berlioz/20 . Date of Habeneck’s Beethoven performances: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Harriet Smithson in Paris, 1827
cues.text: In September 1827 Berlioz saw Harriet Smithson act Shakespeare in Paris, and he fell in love with her before they had met. By 1830 he was writing a symphony about an artist obsessed with his beloved. Smithson heard the revised work in December 1832.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website, Symphonie fantastique, introduction and composition history: Smithson’s 1827 performances and attendance at the concert of 9 December 1832. http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Idée fixe, flute and first violins
cues.text: The flute and first violins play the idée fixe, the fixed idea or obsession, which Berlioz’s 1845 programme identified with the beloved. Its opening G is tied across the barline before the melody rises. Long notes and new starts extend the phrase well beyond four bars.
cues.evidence: Movement I, bars 71–111, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 15–17. Berlioz’s 1845 programme identifies this melody with the beloved: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Paris, 1830
cues.text: On 5 December 1830 Habeneck conducted the première at the Paris Conservatoire. The players gave their services free and had only two rehearsals for the new symphony and Berlioz’s cantata Sardanapale. Three movements caused a sensation; the countryside scene barely registered.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 31, on the première, unpaid players, two rehearsals and the contrasting reception of the movements: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Development, from bar 168
cues.text: In the development the long melody is broken into shorter phrases. The strings begin a figure and the woodwinds reply. Under a held chord the lower strings keep moving, and fragments of the beloved’s melody return throughout.
cues.evidence: Movement I, development from bar 168, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 27–39. The thematic development is discussed at http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Idée fixe in Herminie, 1828
cues.text: The idée fixe first appeared in Herminie, the cantata Berlioz wrote in 1828 for the Prix de Rome. In the symphony he gave the vocal melody to the orchestra. It returns later in the waltz, the march to the execution and the witches’ dance.
cues.evidence: Hector Berlioz Website, Symphonie fantastique, composition history, identifies the borrowing from Herminie; the programme describes the melody’s later appearances. http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/sfantastique.htm

cues.title: Strings against brass chords
cues.text: In the late Allegro, quick string phrases run against broad wind and brass chords. Trumpets and cornets join the horns, and the violins climb high above them. The dynamic rises from forte to fortissimo.
cues.evidence: Movement I, late Allegro, including bars 403–424; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 54–58, shows the climbing strings and sustained wind-and-brass chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing chords, Religiosamente
cues.text: Religiosamente. Woodwinds, horns and strings hold broad chords, marked pianississimo, and the trumpets and cornets rest. The restless string figures stop. Berlioz’s programme ends its account of the movement with the artist’s religious consolation.
cues.evidence: Movement I, bars 513–525, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 71–72; Berlioz’s 1845 programme ends its first-movement account with religious consolation. http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Held G opens the idée fixe
transitions.from: Intro · Muted strings, slow C-minor opening
transitions.to: A · Idée fixe, flute and first violins
transitions.how: The score changes to C major and Allegro agitato e appassionato assai. Emphatic chords are followed by a softer passage in the strings, and the bass descends. Flute and first violins then begin the idée fixe on G. The G is held across a barline, and the melody then rises to C and E.
transitions.evidence: Movement I, bars 64–76, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 14–15: tempo change, descending bass and first statement of the idée fixe. http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas1.pdf

transitions.title: Held chords at Religiosamente
transitions.how: The strings’ moving phrases slow down. At Religiosamente (bar 513), woodwinds, horns and strings hold a succession of quiet chords, marked pianississimo. The timpani punctuate the bass, and the trumpets and cornets rest. The closing progression ends in C major.
transitions.evidence: Movement I, bars 497 to the end, with Religiosamente from bar 513; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 70–72.

source.title: Berlioz, Symphonie fantastique I — orchestral score
source.locator: Largo introduction; first full idée fixe, bars 71–111; development from bar 168; late Allegro; Religiosamente from bar 513.

timeline.note: Flute and clarinet begin the repeated notes; oboe, bassoons and horns join the opening phrase.
Muted first violins play above the other strings, with rests between their phrases.
Wind phrases answer the strings as the slow introduction becomes more animated.
Flute and first violins introduce the idée fixe above a quiet string accompaniment.
Strings and woodwinds exchange fragments of the long melody.
Quick string phrases climb against wind and brass chords.
Winds, horns and strings play the Religiosamente chords quietly, with occasional timpani strokes. The piccolo joins for the final three bars. Trumpets and cornets do not play.

composer.background:
When the young Hector Berlioz read aloud the death of Dido, his voice failed him. His father closed the book and said that he was tired, so the boy did not have to explain his tears. Berlioz recorded the kindness in his Mémoires. Louis Berlioz was a doctor in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, and taught his son Latin, history and geography. He expected Hector to follow him into medicine. The boy learnt the flute and guitar, studied maps of distant islands and was deeply moved by the story of Virgil’s abandoned queen.

In 1821 he went to Paris to study medicine. His first visit to the dissecting room at the Pitié hospital, he later wrote, ended with a flight through a window. On the second visit he managed perfectly well. Music was the more durable obstacle. He heard Salieri’s Les Danaïdes at the Opéra and began singing its airs over the cadavers. At the Conservatoire library he copied and memorised Gluck’s scores. His father argued, threatened and withheld support. Hector took composition lessons with Jean-François Le Sueur.
